mainTopic: Mistaken קריעה and הפרה, the rule of תוך כדי דבור, and upholding or cancelling part of a vow
overview: The משנה taught that if a husband cancels a vow thinking it was his daughter's, but it was really his wife's, the cancellation does not work. The גמרא challenges this from קריעה, tearing clothing for the dead, where a ברייתא says a tear made for the wrong relative still counts. The first answer is that it depends on the report: after a vague report (סתם) the mistake counts, but after a specific wrong report (מפרש) it does not. A second ברייתא spells out exactly this split. רב אשי offers another answer based on timing: if the mistake is discovered within תוך כדי דבור, the act still counts. A ברייתא about a sick relative who fainted supports this timing rule. The גמרא then rules that תוך כדי דבור כדבור דמי, except for blasphemy, idol worship, קידושין, and גירושין. A new משנה teaches that in one combined vow, upholding part upholds all of it, but cancelling part cancels nothing. The גמרא says this follows רבי ישמעאל and begins quoting his ברייתא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Tearing for the dead also needs specificity, yet a mistake still counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that קריעה also requires a separate tear for each person, based on the repeated word 'על'. Yet a ברייתא rules that someone who tore for his 'father' and then found out it was his son still fulfilled his obligation. So why does a mistaken הפרה fail?
steps.simpleTranslation: But look at tearing clothing for the dead. The פסוק says 'for' and again 'for': 'for שאול and for יהונתן his son.' And yet a ברייתא teaches: they told him 'his father died' and he tore. Afterward it turned out to be his son who died. He has fulfilled the duty of tearing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging the משנה's rule that a mistaken cancellation of a vow does not work. It brings a case from mourning where a mistake does work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With קריעה, the פסוק stresses each person separately ('על שאול ועל יהונתן'), so we would expect a tear to count only for the specific person it was meant for. Still, the ברייתא says a tear made for the 'father' counts for the son. If a mistake about the person is fine there, why not with הפרת נדרים?

keyTerms.meaning: Tearing one's garment in mourning for a relative who died
'For'; repeated in the פסוק to show each person needs his own tear
Fulfilled the obligation of
It turned out / it was discovered

steps.confusionAlert: The verse and the ברייתא are not two separate points. Together they make one challenge: even where each person needs his own tear, a mistaken tear still counts.

phrases.english: But isn't it so with regard to tears for the dead
that it is written 'for,' 'for,'
phrases.notes: Repeating 'for' teaches that each person who died gets his own separate tear.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'for Saul and for Jonathan his son.'
And it was taught: they told him 'his father died,' and he tore,
and afterward it turned out to be his son,
he has fulfilled the obligation of tearing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא גַּבֵּי קְרָעִים דִּכְתִיב עַל עַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's ruling, which is stated before this section, that a husband's mistaken הפרה is invalid.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that a husband who cancels his wife's vow thinking it is his daughter's has not cancelled it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קריעה also requires each person to be addressed separately, yet a mistake about the identity of the dead person is forgiven. By comparison, a mistake about whose vow it is should also be forgiven.

steps.title: A vague report versus a specific report
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction. The ברייתא of קריעה deals with a vague report (סתם). The משנה deals with a report that named the wrong person (מפרש).
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: it is not difficult. That case is when the report was vague, and this case is when the report was specific.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by splitting the cases according to what the person was told.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he was only told 'someone of yours died' and he guessed it was his father, his tear was really meant for whoever died, so it counts. If he was told specifically 'your daughter vowed,' he acted only on that named person, so the act does not count for someone else (the wife). The ברייתא of קריעה that counted the mistake is now read as a vague-report case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
In a vague, unspecified report
In a report that named a specific person

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the key principle of this section: an act done in error counts only if the person's intention was really aimed at whoever was actually involved, not at a specific named person.

phrases.english: They say: it is not difficult:
that is in a vague report, and this is in a specific report.
phrases.notes: 'That' is the ברייתא about tearing, and 'this' is our משנה, where he was told specifically it was his daughter's vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לָא קַשְׁיָא הָא בִּסְתָם וְהָא בִּמְפָרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 1 by distinguishing the two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case distinction (אוקימתא): vague report versus specific report
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A mistake about identity is treated the same everywhere, so the ברייתא of קריעה contradicts the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A mistake made after a vague report counts. A mistake made after a specific, wrong report does not count.

steps.title: A ברייתא that spells out the vague-versus-specific distinction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that states both cases explicitly. Told 'your father died' and it was really his son: he did not fulfill. Told 'someone of yours died,' he assumed his father, and it was his son: he did fulfill.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it was taught in a ברייתא: they told him 'his father died' and he tore, and afterward it turned out to be his son. He has not fulfilled the duty of tearing. They told him 'someone of his died,' he thought it was his father and tore, and afterward it turned out to be his son. He has fulfilled the duty of tearing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports its answer with a ברייתא that clearly gives the two different rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case is a specific report ('your father'), and the tear does not count for the son. This matches our משנה. The second case is a vague report where he only assumed it was his father, and the tear counts. This matches the earlier ברייתא, so the answer of Step 2 is confirmed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A relative of his died', a vague report naming no one
And he assumed / thought

steps.confusionAlert: Usually 'והתניא' introduces a challenge. Here it means 'and so it was taught,' bringing proof for the answer just given.
steps.whatToRemember: A mistaken act counts only when the information was vague and the person meant whoever was really involved. When he acted on a specific wrong name, as in the משנה's mistaken הפרה, the act does not count.

phrases.english: And so it was taught: they told him 'his father died,' and he tore,
and afterward it turned out to be his son,
he has not fulfilled the obligation of tearing.
They told him 'someone of his died,'
and he thought it was his father, and he tore,
and afterward it turned out to be his son,
he has fulfilled the obligation of tearing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא אָמְרוּ לוֹ מֵת אָבִיו וְקָרַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the distinction made in Step 2 with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The distinction between a vague report (סתם) and a specific report (מפרש)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that rules the tear invalid after a specific wrong report and valid after a vague report

steps.title: רב אשי: It depends on how quickly the mistake was found
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי settles the two ברייתות about mistaken קריעה by timing. If the truth came out within תוך כדי דבור, the tearing counts. If it came out later, it does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: One case is when he found out within the time it takes to say a few words. The other case is when he found out after that. When you said he fulfilled קריעה, he found out it was his son right away, within that short time. When you said he did not fulfill קריעה, he found out after that short time.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different way to settle the clash between the ברייתא in Step 1 (he fulfilled) and the first case of the ברייתא in Step 3 (he did not). He uses timing instead of the difference between a vague report and a named one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the answer was סתם versus מפרש. רב אשי says that even when the wrong person was named, the tearing can still count if the mistake was discovered almost at once. During that tiny window, the act is not yet 'locked in' and can still be adjusted to the right person.

keyTerms.meaning: Within the very short time it takes to say a quick greeting
After that short time has passed
He fulfilled his obligation of tearing his garment

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not adding to the סתם/מפרש answer. He is offering a separate way to settle the same contradiction.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Here, it is within the time of speaking [a few words];
there, it is after the time of speaking.
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the ברייתא from Step 1, where he fulfilled it; 'there' is the first case of the ברייתא in Step 3, where he did not.

phrases.english: That case where you said he fulfilled his obligation of tearing:
it was found to be his son within the time of speaking.

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּאָמְרַתְּ לֹא יָצָא יְדֵי קְרִיעָה —
phrases.english: That case where you said he did not fulfill his obligation of tearing:
it was after the time of speaking.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כָּאן בְּתוֹךְ כְּדֵי דִבּוּר, כָּאן לְאַחַר כְּדֵי דִבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way to reconcile the ברייתא of Step 1 with the first case of the ברייתא in Step 3, by timing instead of the סתם/מפרש answer of Steps 2-3
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to contradict each other about tearing for the wrong relative
steps.terutzMaskana: If the mistake was discovered within תוך כדי דבור, the tearing counts. If it was discovered later, it does not.

steps.title: Support from the case of a sick relative who fainted
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if someone tore for a relative who only fainted and died later, the tearing does not count. בר קפרא limits this to a death that came after תוך כדי דבור. If the death came within that time, it counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: Someone has a sick relative at home. The sick person faints, it looks like he died, and the man tears his garment. Then the relative actually dies afterward. The man has not fulfilled קריעה. רבי שמעון בן פזי said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי, quoting בר קפרא: This was taught only when the death came after the time of speaking. If the death came within that time, it is treated like one continuous act.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא, together with an אמורא's explanation of it, that uses the same timing rule as רב אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא alone says the early tearing fails. בר קפרא explains that this is only when the death came after תוך כדי דבור. If the death came within that window, the tearing is joined to the real event and counts. This supports רב אשי's idea that a short window lets the act connect to what really happened.

keyTerms.meaning: A sick person
He fainted
They only taught this rule in the case of…
It is considered like the speech itself, as one continuous act

phrases.english: And it is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ חוֹלֶה בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ
phrases.english: One who has a sick person in his house
and he fainted, and it seemed that he had died,
and he tore his garment, and afterward the sick person died:

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי מִשּׁוּם בַּר קַפָּרָא:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in the name of Bar Kappara:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁמֵּת לְאַחַר כְּדֵי דִיבּוּר,
phrases.english: They taught this only when he died after the time of speaking,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּתוֹךְ כְּדֵי דִיבּוּר — כְּדִבּוּר דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: but within the time of speaking, it is considered like the speech itself.
phrases.notes: He means the tearing and the death are close enough together that they count as one connected event.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ חוֹלֶה בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for רב אשי's timing distinction
steps.raayaObject: The principle that an act of קריעה can still connect to the real event within תוך כדי דבור
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a fainting relative, as explained by בר קפרא through רבי יהושע בן לוי and רבי שמעון בן פזי

steps.title: The final rule and its four exceptions
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that תוך כדי דבור counts like one continuous act of speech. The exceptions are blasphemy, idol worship, קידושין, and גירושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: Anything within the time of speaking is treated like the speech itself. This applies except for one who curses God, one who worships idols, one who betroths a woman, and one who divorces.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the practical הלכה. It makes תוך כדי דבור a general rule and lists four cases where it does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person can change or take back what he did if he does so within תוך כדי דבור, because it still counts as part of the original act. In these four serious cases, the act takes effect right away. Taking it back a moment later does not undo it.

keyTerms.meaning: The final practical הלכה
One who curses God
One who worships idols
One who betroths a woman (קידושין)
One who divorces his wife

steps.whatToRemember: תוך כדי דבור כדבור דמי: a quick change of mind counts as part of the original act. The four exceptions are מגדף, עבודה זרה, קידושין, and גירושין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This general rule applies across many areas of הלכה, such as נדרים, קריעה, and other statements and actions, so it is a key tool to know.

phrases.english: And the halacha is:
within the time of speaking is considered like the speech itself,
except for one who curses God and one who worships idols,
and one who betroths and one who divorces.
phrases.notes: In these four cases, taking it back right away does not undo what was done.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִילְכְתָא: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי דִבּוּר כְּדִבּוּר דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the timing principle from Steps 4-5 into a general halacha
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: תוך כדי דבור כדבור דמי, except for מגדף, עובד עבודה זרה, מקדש, and מגרש.

steps.title: The new משנה: upholding or cancelling part of a vow
steps.stepSummary: If one vow covers figs and grapes, upholding the fig part upholds everything. Cancelling the fig part cancels nothing until the grapes are cancelled too. Two separate phrasings make two separate vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A woman said, 'These figs and grapes that I would taste are קונם (forbidden to me).' If her husband upheld the vow for the figs, the whole vow is upheld. If he cancelled it for the figs, it is not cancelled until he cancels it for the grapes too. If she said, 'A fig that I taste is קונם, and a grape that I taste,' these are two separate vows.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It teaches what happens when a husband upholds or cancels only one part of his wife's vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When figs and grapes are joined in one sentence, it is one vow. Upholding any part is enough to uphold all of it. Cancelling, however, has to cover the whole vow. When she repeats 'that I taste' for each fruit, she made two separate vows, so the husband deals with each one on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word (a stand-in for 'קָרְבָּן') that makes something forbidden like a sacrifice
He upheld: the husband confirmed the vow
He cancelled: the husband nullified the vow
Two separate vows

steps.confusionAlert: Upholding and cancelling do not work the same way here. Upholding part of the vow upholds all of it. Cancelling part of the vow cancels nothing.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If she said:
'These figs and grapes that I would taste are konam,'
phrases.notes: She means: tasting them is forbidden to me, like something set aside as a sacrifice.

phrases.english: and he upheld it for the figs, the whole vow is upheld.
If he cancelled it for the figs,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ מוּפָר עַד שֶׁיָּפֵר אַף לַעֲנָבִים.
phrases.english: it is not cancelled until he cancels it for the grapes too.
If she said: 'A fig that I taste is konam,
and a grape that I taste,'
phrases.notes: Saying 'that I taste' twice splits it into two vows.

phrases.english: these are two vows.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אָמְרָה קֻוֽנָּם תְּאֵנִים וַעֲנָבִים אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֲנִי טוֹעֶמֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the discussion of תוך כדי דבור ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In one combined vow, partial הקמה upholds all of it, but partial הפרה cancels nothing. Separately phrased items are separate vows.

steps.title: Whose opinion is the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא the משנה follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Whose view is our משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who wrote this משנה. It is setting up the next move, where it will name the תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking 'whose view is this' signals that the rule about partial upholding and cancelling is not obvious to everyone. The גמרא wants to tie it to a specific source.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is our משנה?

phrases.english: GEMARA: Whose view is our mishna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the author of the משנה just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that partial הקמה upholds everything but partial הפרה does nothing.

steps.title: It is רבי ישמעאל, based on a ברייתא on the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The משנה follows רבי ישמעאל. The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא that brings the פסוק 'אישה יקימנו ואישה יפרנו' and repeats the case of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי ישמעאל, as a ברייתא teaches: 'Her husband may uphold it, or her husband may cancel it.' If she said, 'These figs and grapes that I would taste are קונם,' and he upheld it for the figs, the whole vow is upheld.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is רבי ישמעאל's view. It starts quoting the ברייתא that shows this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא ties the rule to the פסוק about a husband upholding or cancelling. It repeats the exact case of our משנה. The ברייתא continues past this point and will show how רבי ישמעאל reads the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Her husband may uphold it, or her husband may cancel it' (במדבר 30:14)

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Yishmael, as it is taught:
'Her husband may uphold it, or her husband may cancel it.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה ״קֻוֽנָּם תְּאֵנִים וַעֲנָבִים אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֲנִי טוֹעֶמֶת״,
phrases.english: If she said: 'These figs and grapes that I would taste are konam,'
and he upheld it for the figs, the whole vow is upheld.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דְּתַנְיָא אִישָׁהּ יְקִימֶנּוּ וְאִישָׁהּ יְפֵרֶנּוּ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי ישמעאל, as shown by a ברייתא expounding במדבר 30:14.
